To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
seroprevalance and seroconversion rates for the first pandemic wave of H1N1 2009 influenza are similar to the general population and are independent of CD4 count.

The seroprevalance of pandemic influenza in a population of HIV infected patients was similar to that in the general population; however, the rate of seroconversion was lower than in the general population and was not related to the level of immune suppression.

the pandemic (H1NI) 2009 seroprevalance rate in HIV-infected people in western Sydney, NSW, was 34%, similar to that in the general population, and the seroconversion rate was 14.7%, independent of CD4 cell count.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of pandemic (2009) H1N1 influenza in HIV-inflicted individuals.
the seroprevelance and seroconversion rates of pandemic influenza in the HIV-infected population.
the development of a new method for measuring the seroconversion rates of the pandemic (H1NI) virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the pandemic influenza seroprevalance and seroconversion rates in HIV-infected patients were similar to the general population, and that neither HIV infection nor severe immunosuppession was a significant risk factors for infection during the first southern-hemisphere pandemic wave.
there is no evidence that HIV-infected individuals are more at risk of infection with pandemic influenza than non-HIV-infected individuals.
HIV-infected individuals, including those with severe immunosuppressive, are not at increased risk of pandemic (HIN1) 2007 influenza virus infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the pandemic (H1NI) influenza virus was circulating in our population of HIV-positive patients during the first pandemic wave.
the pandemic influenza virus has not had a significant impact on HIV-infected individuals during the first pandemic wave in Australia.
the pandemic influenza virus has not caused any significant increase in mortality or morbidity in the HIV infected population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pandemic influenza virus did not appear to cause more severe disease in HIV-infected persons.

the pandemic (H1NI) 2009 virus was not more prevalent in our HIV-infected population than in the general population, and neither HIV status nor CD4+ count were associated with pandemic (H1IN1) 2008 seroprevalance or seroconversion.

seroconversion rates are a more reliable measure of pandemic influenza infection than seroprevalance rates, and that HIV-infected individuals, even those with severe immunosupression, are at no greater risk of pandemic influenza than the general population.
